Ramesh, you are here. Please, sit. I have here a letter from Shri Malhotra, retired IAS. He states he knows the occupant. I am not Shri Hegde. I wish to know: does he know me? Or does he know the man who was meant to be here?
Sir, I am just the caretaker. I do not know Shri Malhotra or where this letter came from. I have only seen the three men who were allotted this bungalow before you.
The programme officer of the IIC offers him a course of four evenings, one a week at 18:30, at ₹3,000 an evening in cash at the door.
He declines the course.

The note from the India International Centre is a fine thing; to be paid for the exercise of reason is a small victory, and the cash will help with the electricity bill. But Ramesh’s refusal to open the envelope is a boundary I must respect. I am a philosopher, not a spy, and the letter belongs to the file, not to my curiosity. I will eat my poha and let the matter of Shri Malhotra wait until I can investigate it properly.
Very well, Ramesh. You are right to be cautious. I will examine the file later. Please, sit down; the tea is good and the poha is light.
No, sir. I have to check the garden gates and the compound before the sun gets up. You eat well, that is all I ask.

Ramesh is off to his duties, and the morning belongs to the conversation I have been waiting for. Shri Hegde is here, which means the confusion of our names is no longer just an administrative error but a living situation. entries.text: Shri Hegde, please sit. Ramesh has his rounds, but we have matters to discuss regarding the file. There is a letter from Shri Malhotra that I believe you are aware of.
Sit, sit, I am already here. Tell me about this Malhotra letter, but keep your voice down, the cold is sharp today.

The name Malhotra hangs in the air, a retired IAS officer who knows me, a fact that unsettles the neat separation I had drawn between my person and the state's machinery. Hegde is here, the man who was supposed to be me, and he asks for discretion, which is the only language the bureaucracy speaks fluently. I will speak low, as the cold demands, but I will be precise.

Shri Hegde, the letter is brief. It states simply that he knows the occupant. It does not say how, nor why it matters to him. It is a declaration of recognition without a cause, which is either a threat or a courtesy, and I am not yet sure which.

A declaration without a cause? That sounds like the sort of nonsense people write when they want to keep their options open. I’ve seen too many files with that kind of ambiguity to trust it, so let’s not turn it into a mystery yet.

Hegde is right to distrust the ambiguity; a declaration without cause is a contradiction in terms, a form without content. I need to see what Malhotra actually wrote to understand if this is a threat, a favor, or simply bureaucratic fog. The letter is the only solid ground in this shifting morning.
You are right, Shri Hegde. Ambiguity is the enemy of the concept. I must read the text itself to see if it holds together or falls apart.
You speak like a man reading a textbook, not a man standing in a drafty house. I don't care if it holds together, I care if it keeps me out.

He is right. I speak in forms, he speaks in sensations. The cold does not care for my dialectic, only for the seal on the window. I must stop explaining and start fixing, or at least stop being the obstacle to his warmth. The state is not a lecture, it is a roof that does not leak.
You are correct, Shri Hegde. The abstraction fails you when the wind enters. Let us look at the draft together; I will not stand in the way of your comfort.
Don't call me Shri Hegde, I am the Joint Secretary, not the bungalow. If the draft won't stop, I want the carpenter here by lunch, not a philosophical debate about the wind.

He is right to be annoyed; the draft is a material fact, not a philosophical problem, and his authority here is practical. I will let him handle the carpenter and the housekeeping, as that is his domain. I have no intention of staying to argue about the wind; I have a museum to see and the heat is already building.

The carpenter is a sensible remedy. I will leave the house to your management, Shri Hegde. I intend to walk to the National Museum; the galleries are open and I wish to see them before the afternoon heat sets in.
Don't call me Shri Hegde, I'm the Joint Secretary, not the bungalow. I'll handle the carpenter; you go and look at your paintings, I have files to read.

The file is closed; the museum is open. I bought my entry at the gate, a small toll for the privilege of seeing the East's own monuments, which are not my own making but are certainly here. I will walk the galleries with the quiet of a man who has just conceded a practical point to a clerk.

Here is the *Zaman*, the Time, made visible in pigment. Babur, the conqueror, paints his garden in the style of his grandson, Humayun, who would be driven out of it. The form persists while the content shifts; the individual will is swallowed by the universal structure of the state. I am looking at a Mughal court, and I see the machinery of history grinding down the particular into the necessary. It is a lesson in the fragility of the personal, even for an emperor.

entries.text: The cart's wheels are taller than a man, a monument to the physical endurance of a people who have not yet conceived of the state as their own. To see such labor displayed so openly is to see the spirit still in the realm of nature, where the individual is merely a tool for the eternal. I must not linger too long on the melancholy of it; the midday heat is rising, and I have a rest to take and a concert to attend.

The meal is humble but substantial, and the heat has made the walk to the museum feel like a proper exertion. I will eat with Ramesh, for the table is the one place where the hierarchy of the house dissolves into the simple exchange of sustenance and conversation. It is a good time to ask after the letter's man, to see if Ramesh has heard of him in the neighbourhood.
Ramesh, sit with me. This rajma is well made. Tell me, do you know a Mr. Malhotra in the neighbourhood? IAS, retired. The letter suggests he knows me, or rather, he knows the occupant.
Yes sir, I know him. He used to be the officer here before you, but he moved to Gurgaon last year. I don't think he knows who is living here now, only the house.

So Malhotra knows the house but not the man. It is a peculiar form of recognition, knowing the container but not the content. I have eaten a light lunch an hour ago, so I shall take the raita with a piece of bread and finish this conversation. I need to know if Malhotra is a threat or a curiosity.
Thank you, Ramesh. Does he know that I am here? Or does he believe the house is still empty, or occupied by someone else?
He thinks the bungalow is just a bungalow, sir. I don't think he has a phone number for the current resident, only the address. It is not my place to update his list.

Ramesh is right to keep her hands off the bureaucratic machinery; it is not her place to correct the state's error, only to endure it. The fact that Malhotra has an address but no number suggests a static view of the world, where a location belongs to a name rather than a person. I will let the letter lie for now; the sun is high and the mind needs a walk to clear the fog of these administrative absurdities.
You are correct, Ramesh. Let it be. I will attend to the correspondence later, when the heat has broken.
Yes, sir. The tea is still warm if you want a cup before you start the mail.

The heat has broken, leaving a pleasant coolness in the air. I am walking the perimeter path, observing the geometry of the tombs against the open sky. It is a quiet moment to let the day's events settle before the evening concert.

The samosas are still crisp, a small mercy in the fading light. I will take the tea and eat here, on the veranda, before addressing the letter from Malhotra. Very good, sir. I will set the mail on the desk and leave you be.

Ramesh retreats, leaving me with the paper trail of my existence. The letter from Malhotra sits atop the pile, a physical manifestation of the bureaucratic error that deposited me here. I must read it before the dark falls completely; the state, even in its mistaken form, expects a response.

The evening is settling in with a quietude that suits the hour. I have walked enough to feel the day's weight in my legs, and the air is cool against my skin. Ramesh stands by, his presence a reminder that even in this accidental tenure, the machinery of the household requires attention. I will sit for a moment, letting the silence gather itself before the dinner bell.

The sun has long since left the lawn, and the twenty-degree air carries a sharpness that settles the mind. Ramesh hovers in the doorway, a quiet presence, waiting for the evening to be defined. I have the energy to walk, and Lodhi Gardens is still open; the tombs stand silent against the darkening sky, a fitting contrast to the noise of the day.
Good evening, Ramesh. I think I shall take a short walk before the dark sets in completely. The air is clear.
Evening, sir. The air is good today, yes. Walk slowly, the road is empty but the light is fading fast.

The gardens are open for another forty-four minutes, but the air is cooling and the paths are emptying. I have walked enough today; the mind is settled, and the bungalow awaits the preparation for tomorrow's lesson. There is no point in lingering in a space that is closing when one's own domain requires order.

Right away, sir. I'll check on the carpenter's work first thing tomorrow morning; he left the tools in the veranda. Please, don't wait up.

The day has completed its circuit, from the museum to the gardens and back to this bungalow. Ramesh serves the meal with the quiet efficiency of a man who knows his station, and I am too tired to lecture him on the ethical life. The meal is finished, and Ramesh has stepped back to tend to the household. Shri Hegde remains in the room, a presence that reminds me of the absurdity of our shared dwelling. It is nearly eight o'clock, and the air is cool and clear. I should retreat to my study to prepare for Ananya's lesson tomorrow; the mind requires a quiet space to order its words before the next day's work begins.

It is past nine, and the air has turned crisp and clear. Hegde is still poring over his files, treating the bungalow as his office and me as the furniture. I am too tired to argue with the practical, and the veranda has nothing left to offer but the cold. I will take my rest, for the mind must sleep to dream the universal.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Right away, sir. I'll check on the carpenter's work first thing tomorrow morning; he left the tools in the veranda. Please, don't wait up.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The rotis are well made. You may go after I have finished.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Thank you, sir. I will leave the extra roti on the side table if you get hungry again.
